title: Akkad and the Third Dynasty of Ur
subtitle: 2334–2004 BC · The First Empire, the God-King Naram-Sin, the Gutian Interlude, and the Bureaucratic Renaissance of Ur

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Sargon's Akkad and the first empire, the self-deification of Naram-Sin, the Gutian interlude and Gudea's Lagash, and the bureaucratic renaissance and swift fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur

entries.label: Sargon founds the first empire
entries.hint: Sargon rose as cup-bearer to the king of Kish, seized power, and built a new capital, Akkad, whose site has never been found. He defeated Lugalzagesi and the kings of Sumer, campaigned to the cedar mountains and the Mediterranean, washed his weapons in the Lower Sea, and installed his daughter Enheduanna as priestess at Ur. He ruled the whole of Mesopotamia for over fifty years — the first man to weld it into one state and hold it.
entries.note: Douglas Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016); the later 'Sargon Birth Legend' edited by Brian Lewis (1980).

entries.label: Rimush and Manishtushu — revolt and consolidation
entries.hint: Sargon's sons inherited a rebellion. Rimush put down a general Sumerian revolt with a slaughter his own inscriptions tally by the tens of thousands, and was then murdered by his courtiers. Manishtushu raided across the Gulf against thirty-two kings of Magan and left an obelisk recording enormous royal purchases of land — the crown turning conquest into permanent estates.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); the Manishtushu Obelisk (Louvre) in Gelb, Steinkeller & Whiting, 'Earliest Land Tenure Systems in the Near East' (1991).

entries.label: Naram-Sin, god of Akkad
entries.hint: Naram-Sin, Sargon's grandson, crushed a 'Great Revolt' of Kish, Uruk and a wide coalition, claiming nine battles won in a single year. In its wake the citizens of Akkad asked the gods to make him their city-god: he wrote his name with the sign for 'divine', wore the horned crown of a deity, and styled himself 'King of the Four Quarters'. He campaigned from Anatolia to Magan and destroyed Ebla and Armanum in Syria.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); the deification analysed in Piotr Michalowski, 'The Mortal Kings of Ur' (2008); the 'Great Revolt' text in Old Babylonian copies (Aage Westenholz).

entries.label: Shar-kali-sharri and the unravelling
entries.hint: Shar-kali-sharri dropped the grand title and called himself simply 'king of Akkad'. He fought the Gutians in the Zagros, the Elamites in the east and the Amorites in the west, and rebuilt the Ekur at Nippur. After him the empire dissolved into a scramble the King List records as a bitter question: 'Who was king? Who was not king?'
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); the interregnum in the Sumerian King List (Jacobsen 1939) and Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016).

entries.label: The Gutians hold the land
entries.loc: the Zagros piedmont and the central plain
entries.hint: A people from the Zagros mountains, the Gutians raided the collapsing empire and then loosely dominated its centre and north for two or three generations. Later Sumerian texts cast them as barbarians 'who knew no inhibitions', and blame them for ruin and famine. How much they actually governed is unclear — many southern cities, Lagash above all, ran their own affairs and prospered.
entries.note: W. W. Hallo, 'Gutium' (Reallexikon der Assyriologie III); the hostile tradition in 'The Curse of Agade' (Cooper 1983) and the Utu-hegal inscription.

entries.label: Gudea of Lagash, the builder
entries.hint: While the north lay under the Gutians, Lagash under its governor Gudea was independent and rich, trading for cedar from the Amanus, diorite from Magan and copper and carnelian from farther still. Gudea spent his reign rebuilding the temple of Ningirsu, the Eninnu, an undertaking he recorded on two great clay cylinders — the longest Sumerian literary text — and commemorated in some two dozen statues of himself carved from imported black stone.
entries.note: Dietz Otto Edzard, RIME 3/1: 'Gudea and His Dynasty' (1997); the Cylinders translated in Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Harps That Once...' (1987).

entries.label: Utu-hegal drives out the Gutians
entries.hint: Utu-hegal, king of Uruk, marched against the Gutian king Tirigan, defeated and captured him, and 'set his foot on his neck' — ending, in his own telling, the kingship of Gutium and returning it to Sumer. His victory inscription is the main source for the episode. He reigned only a few years before his own appointed governor of Ur, Ur-Namma, eclipsed him.
entries.note: The Utu-hegal inscription in Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); Jacob Klein, 'Šulgi and Išme-Dagan' and studies of the Uruk V dynasty.

entries.label: Ur-Namma founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
entries.hint: Ur-Namma, governor of Ur, made himself king and reunited Sumer and Akkad under his city. He rebuilt the great temples and raised the first true stepped ziggurats at Ur, Uruk, Eridu and Nippur; he issued the earliest law code known; and he dug and cleared canals. He died in a battle against the Gutians, his body left on the field — a shock a Sumerian lament struggled to reconcile with divine justice.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 3/2 (1997); the 'Death of Ur-Namma' lament translated by Jacob Klein; the law code in Martha Roth, 'Law Collections' (1997).

entries.label: Shulgi and the machine state
entries.hint: In a reign of nearly fifty years Shulgi rebuilt the state as a bureaucracy: a rotating provincial tax (the bala), a central livestock clearing-house at Puzrish-Dagan, standard weights, a fixed calendar, a courier relay, reorganised armies and a scribal school. Around year twenty he had himself declared a god. The hymns in his name praise his running, his letters, his music and his judgements; the archives his reforms generated make Ur III the best-documented state of the Bronze Age.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 3/2 (1997); the reforms in Piotr Steinkeller, 'The Administrative and Economic Organization of the Ur III State' (1987); the Shulgi hymns edited by Jacob Klein.

entries.label: Amar-Sin and Shu-Sin
entries.hint: Under Shulgi's successors the deified-king cult reached its height — temples and statues of the living king stood in every province and received offerings. Amar-Sin campaigned in the Zagros and rebuilt Eridu. Shu-Sin built a fortified line across the waist of Mesopotamia, Muriq-Tidnim, 'the wall that keeps out the Tidnum', against the Amorite nomads pressing in from the west. It did not hold for long.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 3/2 (1997); the wall and the Amorite pressure in Piotr Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011).

entries.label: Ibbi-Sin and the fall of Ur
entries.hint: The empire came apart around Ibbi-Sin in stages: the eastern provinces stopped sending their bala, Ishbi-Erra — an officer sent north to buy grain — set himself up as an independent king at Isin, the Amorites overran the fields, and the price of barley in Ur rose sixtyfold. In 2004 the Elamites and the men of Shimashki stormed the city, carried off the moon-god's statue, and led Ibbi-Sin in chains to Anshan. It was the end of Sumerian imperial rule.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011); 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur' (Michalowski 1989).

entries.label: 'King of the Four Quarters' — the claim to universal rule
entries.hint: Naram-Sin replaced the old claim to lead 'the land' with a new one: 'King of the Four Quarters' (šar kibrāt arbaim), ruler of the whole inhabited world to its edges. Coupled with the living king's divinity, it made kingship cosmic rather than civic. Ur III revived both — Shu-Sin was a god and King of the Four Quarters — and the pairing became a template that Assyrian and Babylonian kings would reach for two thousand years later.
entries.note: Titulary in William Hallo, 'Early Mesopotamian Royal Titles' (1957); the ideology in Mario Liverani (ed.), 'Akkad: The First World Empire' (1993).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Sargon's conquest of Sumer, the Great Revolt against Naram-Sin, the Gutian incursions and the fall of Akkad, the Amorite wall, and the sack of Ur by Elam

entries.label: Sargon's conquest of Sumer
entries.loc: from Kish to the Lower Sea
entries.hint: Sargon defeated Lugalzagesi of Uruk in a great battle, brought him in a neck-stock to the gate of Enlil at Nippur, and then reduced the other Sumerian cities one by one — 'fifty governors', by his count — dismantling their walls and washing his weapons in the Persian Gulf. It was the first campaign to bring the whole of Sumer and Akkad under a single ruler and keep it there.
entries.note: Sargon's inscriptions in Frayne, RIME 2 (1993); narrative in Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016).

entries.label: The Great Revolt against Naram-Sin
entries.hint: A coalition led by Kish and Uruk and reaching into the north and the Gulf rose against Naram-Sin. His inscriptions claim nine victories in one year and three captured kings; the Old Babylonian literary tradition made the revolt a set-piece of royal endurance. Its suppression is the event that immediately precedes Naram-Sin's deification — the king saved the city, so the city made him its god.
entries.note: The 'Great Revolt' inscriptions and their later copies in Aage Westenholz's studies; Frayne, RIME 2 (1993).

entries.label: The Gutians and the fall of Akkad
entries.hint: Through and after Shar-kali-sharri's reign the Gutians raided from the Zagros, the harvests failed, and the city of Akkad shrank and finally vanished so completely that it has never been located. The poem 'The Curse of Agade' explains the catastrophe as Enlil's revenge for Naram-Sin's supposed sacking of the Ekur at Nippur — the first attempt to give a historical disaster a theological cause.
entries.note: Jerrold Cooper, 'The Curse of Agade' (1983); the archaeology of the Akkadian collapse in Harvey Weiss's work and Foster (2016).

entries.label: Utu-hegal defeats Tirigan
entries.hint: Utu-hegal of Uruk marched out against the last Gutian king, Tirigan, praying to Inanna and to the war-god as he went, defeated him, took him and his family captive, and made him lie face down while the king set a foot on his neck. His inscription presents the victory as the liberation of the whole land and the return of kingship to Sumer.
entries.note: The Utu-hegal victory inscription in Frayne, RIME 2 (1993).

entries.label: Shu-Sin's wall against the Amorites
entries.hint: To stop the Amorite (MAR.TU) nomads filtering out of the Syrian steppe into the farmland, Shu-Sin built a fortified line, Muriq-Tidnim, running roughly between the Tigris and the Euphrates north of the cities. Garrisoning it strained the treasury, letters from the frontier officers plead for men and grain, and within a generation the Amorites were through it and inside the realm.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011); the wall's route debated (Vincente; Michalowski).

entries.label: The sack of Ur
entries.hint: The collapse under Ibbi-Sin compounded: provincial defection, Ishbi-Erra's secession at Isin and his grain blackmail, Amorite raiding, famine and a sixtyfold rise in the price of barley. The finish came from the east — an army of Elam and Shimashki took Ur, burned it, plundered the temples, carried the statue of the moon-god Nanna and the king himself away to Anshan, and left a garrison in the ruins.
entries.note: 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur' (Michalowski 1989); the sequence in Michalowski, 'The Correspondence of the Kings of Ur' (2011).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The first imperial administration and the empire-wide year-name, Naram-Sin's godhood as a governing act, the Ur III command state and its bala tax, and the Code of Ur-Namma

entries.label: The first imperial administration
entries.hint: Sargon governed the conquered cities through his own appointees and 'citizens of Akkad', kept a standing corps of 5,400 men who 'ate bread daily before him', and made Akkadian the language of the chancery. The whole empire dated its documents by year-names proclaimed from the capital. It was the first working answer to the problem of ruling many cities from one — improvised, personal, and only as strong as the king.
entries.note: Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016); Aage Westenholz, 'The Old Akkadian Period: History and Culture' (1999).

entries.label: Deification as a constitutional act
entries.hint: Making the living king a god was not merely flattery: it lifted him clear of the councils of city elders and the temple hierarchies that a mortal ensi had to work with, made an oath in his name a religious act, and entitled his statues to offerings. Naram-Sin's innovation gave the crown a new kind of authority, and Ur III would take it up as deliberate policy.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Mortal Kings of Ur' (2008); the ideological mechanics in Gebhard Selz's studies of Sumerian divine kingship.

entries.label: The Manishtushu Obelisk and the royal estate
entries.loc: Found: Susa (carried off later) · Now: Musée du Louvre
entries.hint: A four-sided stone monument records King Manishtushu buying eight large estates — thousands of hectares — from communities of landholders, paying in silver, barley, wool, oil and copper, and feasting the sellers. Whether coerced or willing, the transactions turned a patchwork of family and village land into consolidated crown estates worked by dependent labour: a lasting change in who owned Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Ignace Gelb, Piotr Steinkeller & Robert Whiting, 'Earliest Land Tenure Systems in the Near East: Ancient Kudurrus' (OIP 104, 1991).

entries.label: The bala — a command economy by rotation
entries.hint: Under Shulgi each province paid into a central pool on a fixed rota — grain, cattle, wool, reeds, craft goods, gangs of workers — and drew from it in return as the state directed. Ur and its clearing-houses matched the flows and recorded every transfer. It was a genuine planned redistribution across the whole realm, and it generated the tens of thousands of tablets that make Ur III the best-known state of the age.
entries.note: Piotr Steinkeller, 'The Administrative and Economic Organization of the Ur III State' (1987); Tonia Sharlach, 'Provincial Taxation and the Ur III State' (2004).

entries.label: The Code of Ur-Namma
entries.hint: The oldest law collection that survives opens with the king proclaiming that he has set right weights, protected the orphan from the rich and the widow from the powerful, and freed the land of tyranny — then lists some forty rulings. Many injuries are settled in weighed silver rather than by the eye-for-an-eye that Hammurabi's laws would impose three centuries later. Law is presented as a gift the just king makes to his people.
entries.note: Martha Roth, 'Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor' (1997), pp. 13–22; first edition by Samuel Noah Kramer (1954).

entries.label: The ensi, the shagina and the audit
entries.loc: the provinces of the Ur III realm
entries.hint: Each province had two governors watching each other: a civil ensi, often local and hereditary, and a military shagina, an outsider loyal to the king. Weights, the calendar and sealed authorisations were standardised across the realm, a courier relay of ration-points moved orders and men, and every official's account was audited — a shortfall was booked against him and, if he died owing, pursued against his heirs.
entries.note: Steinkeller (1987); the audit and debt-after-death practice in Steven Garfinkle, 'Entrepreneurs and Enterprise in Early Mesopotamia' (2012).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Ishtar the patron of Akkad, the deified living king, Enheduanna and the first authored hymns, Gudea's temple theology, and the ziggurats of the Ur III revival

entries.label: Ishtar, patron of the dynasty
entries.hint: Sargon and Naram-Sin credited their fortunes to Ishtar in her warlike aspect, Annunitum, and built her temples in the capital. Under Akkadian patronage the Sumerian Inanna and the Semitic Ishtar fused into a single supreme goddess of sexual love and of battle — the most vividly characterised deity in the Mesopotamian pantheon, and the one the empire made its own.
entries.note: Benjamin Foster, 'The Age of Agade' (2016), ch. 5; Brigitte Groneberg's studies of the goddess Ishtar.

entries.label: The living king as a god
entries.hint: From Naram-Sin, and as settled policy from Shulgi, the reigning king was a god: his name written with the divine sign, his image crowned with horns, temples and priesthoods dedicated to him, offerings burned before his statue, and ordinary people named 'Shulgi-is-my-god'. It was theology in the service of the state, and it did not survive the fall of Ur — later kings claimed divine favour, not divinity.
entries.note: Piotr Michalowski, 'The Mortal Kings of Ur' (2008); the deified-king cult in Walther Sallaberger, 'Der kultische Kalender der Ur III-Zeit' (1993).

entries.label: Enheduanna, the first named author
entries.hint: Sargon set his daughter Enheduanna over the temple of the moon-god at Ur as its en-priestess, an office that fused politics and cult. She composed a cycle of 42 hymns to the temples of the land and a long poem to Inanna in which she names herself, describes being driven from her office during a rebellion, and begs the goddess to restore her. She is the earliest author in world literature known by name — and a woman.
entries.note: William Hallo & J. J. A. van Dijk, 'The Exaltation of Inanna' (1968); Sophus Helle, 'Enheduana: The Complete Poems' (2023).

entries.label: Gudea's temple theology
entries.loc: Found: Girsu (Telloh) · Now: Musée du Louvre
entries.hint: Gudea's two clay cylinders tell how the god Ningirsu appeared to him in a dream and demanded a temple, how a goddess interpreted the dream and a god gave him the plan, and how the Eninnu was then built and consecrated, described chamber by chamber, until heaven and earth were set in order. It is the fullest surviving statement of the Mesopotamian idea that a temple is a cosmic instrument and its building a sacred duty.
entries.note: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Harps That Once...' (1987), pp. 386–444; Claudia Suter, 'Gudea's Temple Building' (2000).

entries.label: The ziggurat and the moon-god of Ur
entries.hint: Ur-Namma raised for the moon-god Nanna a solid stepped tower of mud brick faced in baked brick set in bitumen, its base sixty metres on a side, climbed by a triple monumental stair — the first true ziggurat, and the model for all the rest. Rebuilding Nanna's house and the ruined temples of the other cities was a founding act of the dynasty, which took the moon-god as its own.
entries.note: Leonard Woolley, 'Ur Excavations V: The Ziggurat and Its Surroundings' (1939); the Ur III temple programme in Sallaberger (1993).

entries.label: Reading the will of the gods in the liver
entries.hint: The Akkadian and Ur III periods see the first clear evidence for extispicy — putting a question to the gods, sacrificing a sheep, and reading the answer in the markings of its liver and lungs. Clay models of ominous livers and the earliest omen sentences ('if the gall-bladder is turned — the enemy will...') appear now. It became the central procedure of Mesopotamian statecraft, consulted before every campaign and appointment for two thousand years.
entries.note: Clay liver models from Mari and elsewhere; Ulla Koch, 'Secrets of Extispicy' (2005); early omens in the studies of Abraham Winitzer.
